runs.task: Survey recent arXiv work on the higgsino thermal relic target (1.0-1.2 TeV). Use the inelastic-DM tools to compute the relic density at several masses; compare with LZ/XENONnT sensitivities and the Planck abundance. Where does the higgsino sit relative to current limits?

brief.summary: Note first: I did not compute any relic densities. No inelastic-DM or relic-density tools were available to me, only literature search tools, so everything below comes from paper abstracts. Second note: the 'recent arXiv work' shown here was found through the OpenAlex-backed search_arxiv tool, which returned papers dated June to October 2026. These IDs should be checked on arxiv.org before anyone cites them. The direct arXiv API search_arxiv_abstracts tool returned HTTP 503/429 errors. On the physics: when the Sommerfeld effect and coannihilation are included, a pure higgsino gives the full Planck abundance at m about 1.0-1.2 TeV. The cited values are about 1.08-1.1 TeV (2609.02775, 2609.02608), about 1.2 TeV (2410.15733) and an upper end near 1150 GeV (2403.19598). Lighter thermal higgsinos are under-abundant, typically by a factor of 5-20 in natural SUSY (1803.11210). For direct detection, the pure higgsino is inelastic dark matter: its Z-mediated scattering requires a neutral-state mass splitting delta of up to about a few hundred keV. If delta is larger than the kinematic reach of xenon, elastic loop-level scattering sits near or below the neutrino fog (2609.01504, 2410.02723). Higgsino-gaugino mixing raises the elastic rate and is what lets direct detection probe the thermal target (2606.31013). In 2026, LZ released a 2.84 tonne-year search with an extended nuclear-recoil window (2609.02823). It found one event at 248 keV, with 2.6 sigma global and 3.4 sigma local significance. A roughly 1.1 TeV higgsino with delta of about 340-380 keV under the Standard Halo Model, or about 480-520 keV if the Large Magellanic Cloud's effect on the halo velocity tail is included, can produce this event. However, IceCube solar-capture neutrino limits require delta > 566 keV (2609.02775, confirmed by 2609.11833 and 2609.07807; 2609.06760 quotes 0.51-0.56 MeV). Two further problems: the empty sideband above 350 keV is in tension with the thermal-mass fit (2609.09385, 2609.26698), and halo uncertainties are not enough to close the gap (2609.15321). Bottom line: the full-abundance thermal higgsino at about 1.1 TeV is not excluded as a model. Its sub-MeV-splitting interpretation of the LZ event is disfavoured by solar capture. Splittings of order an MeV or more remain allowed (2610.00226) and leave it effectively out of reach of current xenon searches. Indirect gamma-ray line searches (CTA/CTAO, 2008.00692) are the main future test.

literature.title: Search for dark matter particle interactions in an extended nuclear recoil energy window with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment
literature.relevance: Primary LZ result: 2.84 tonne-year exposure, recoil window up to about 270 keV, one event at 248 keV (2.6 sigma global, 3.4 sigma local). This is the reference dataset for inelastic higgsino limits.

literature.title: Strong Constraints on Higgsino Dark Matter from Solar Capture
literature.relevance: Uses the thermal mass m about 1.08 TeV. IceCube non-observation gives delta > 566 keV, which excludes the endothermic higgsino explanation of the LZ event.

literature.title: Higgsino Above the Sea of Fog
literature.relevance: Overview of the 1.1 TeV thermal higgsino as inelastic DM. Preferred delta is about 350 keV under the Standard Halo Model and about 500 keV with the LMC; delta of several hundred keV implies gauginos at about 10^3-10^4 TeV.

literature.title: Dark Matter at the Kinematic Edge: Interpreting the 248 keV LZ Nuclear-Recoil Candidate
literature.relevance: Relic abundance fixes the higgsino mass near 1.1 TeV; delta about 377 keV reproduces the event. Uses published LZ efficiencies. Also gives a pseudo-Dirac benchmark (1 TeV, sigma_N about 6.5e-43 cm^2, delta about 297 keV).

literature.title: Heavy Higgsino Interpretation of the LZ Event
literature.relevance: Fits (m, delta) to the event plus the empty sideband above 350 keV. At the 1.1 TeV thermal mass, several sideband events are predicted and none are seen. Recomputes solar-capture limits as a function of mass.

literature.title: Model-Independent Sideband Constraints on Inelastic Dark Matter at the LZ High-Recoil Candidate
literature.relevance: Sideband count ratios across (m, delta). At 1 TeV the optimal delta is 339 keV, with about 1.9 sigma tension. Shows the Helm form factor suppression at 248 keV. Directly reproducible.

literature.title: Confronting the Higgsino Interpretation of the LZ Event with Astrophysical Uncertainties and the Solar Capture Constraints
literature.relevance: Under the Standard Halo Model, delta > 566 keV requires v0 > 240 km/s. In a simulated halo with the LMC, delta = 514 keV is the largest splitting that still gives one event in 200-300 keV. Concludes halo uncertainties cannot reconcile the higgsino with solar-capture limits.

literature.title: TeV Higgsino Dark Matter from LZ Nuclear Recoil to Fermi-LAT Gamma Rays
literature.relevance: With the LMC tail, finds delta = 481-519 keV for m = 1000-1183 GeV. Their IceCube treatment excludes delta < 475 keV. Gives a gamma-line prediction for CTAO.

literature.title: Solar Capture Tests of Inelastic Dark Matter after the LZ High-Recoil Event
literature.relevance: Independent solar-capture analysis: the full-density thermal higgsino needs delta > 0.51-0.56 MeV, versus the LZ-preferred value of about 0.38 MeV.

literature.title: Solar Neutrino Constraints on Inelastic Dark Matter Scattering in Light of Recent LUX-ZEPLIN Observations
literature.relevance: Independent confirmation of the Pospelov-Ramani solar-capture bound.

literature.title: Thermal Higgsino Dark Matter in GmSUGRA for the LZ Event and Solar-Neutrino Constraint
literature.relevance: A Planck-compatible thermal higgsino branch survives at delta of about 0.85-1.34 MeV, above the solar-capture limits.

literature.title: Implications of purity constraints on light Higgsinos
literature.relevance: The thermal higgsino must lie between about 100 and 1150 GeV. Gives purity constraints: lower bounds on gaugino masses and upper bounds on the higgsino mass splittings.

literature.title: Non-thermal production of Higgsino dark matter by late-decaying scalar fields
literature.relevance: Thermal relic mass of about 1.2 TeV with Sommerfeld and coannihilation included. Shows how the mass shifts with a low reheating temperature.

literature.title: Is natural higgsino-only dark matter excluded?
literature.relevance: Lighter higgsinos are under-abundant by a factor of 5-20. Topping them up non-thermally to the full abundance was already constrained by earlier xenon and Fermi/MAGIC data.

literature.title: Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection
literature.relevance: Direct detection reaches the 1 TeV thermal higgsino only when higgsino-gaugino mixing is non-negligible.

literature.title: Looking for WIMPs through the neutrino fogs
literature.relevance: Exposures that xenon detectors need for electroweak WIMPs, including both neutrino fogs. Context for elastic higgsino reach.

literature.title: Prospects for detecting heavy WIMP dark matter with the Cherenkov Telescope Array: The Wino and Higgsino
literature.relevance: CTA could be the first experiment sensitive to the thermal higgsino through indirect detection.

literature.title: A Warped Extra Dimensional Candidate for the LZ 248 keV Event
literature.relevance: Summarises the solar-capture and sideband tensions for the thermal higgsino and proposes a non-higgsino inelastic DM alternative.

directions.goal: Compute the thermal relic density Omega h^2 of a higgsino-like (inelastic) DM candidate at m = 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV with the inelastic-DM tools. Compare each value with Planck (Omega h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001) and locate the mass where the tool's relic curve crosses the Planck abundance.
directions.rationale: This answers the core quantitative part of the task directly. The survey computed no relic densities. Its literature crossing point of about 1.08-1.2 TeV needs a tool-based cross-check, and we need to know which physics the tool includes (Sommerfeld effect, coannihilation, higgsino couplings).
steps: Call describe_tools first. Record the model the server implements: couplings, whether it is higgsino-specific or generic inelastic DM, whether Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation are included, parameter names, units and validity range. Quote these verbatim in the finding.

Call compute_relic_density at m_chi = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV, with a fixed representative splitting (for example delta = 0.4 MeV, or the schema's default; check the units in the schema). Pass a distinct label per mass if the tool accepts one.
If the tool exposes a Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, repeat the 1000, 1100 and 1200 GeV points with it toggled. This gives the with/without comparison.
Check sensitivity to the splitting: at m_chi = 1100 GeV, compute the relic density for delta = 0.3, 0.566 and 1.0 MeV, if those values are in range.
Tabulate Omega h^2 against mass. Interpolate the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120 and give its uncertainty from the +/-0.001 Planck band.
Call check_all_constraints at m_chi = 1100 GeV, delta = 0.4 MeV, and at the interpolated crossing mass. Record the relic, LZ, Fermi-LAT and Planck CMB verdicts.

Compare the tool's crossing mass with the literature values (about 1.08-1.1 TeV in 2609.02775 and 2609.02608; about 1.2 TeV in 2410.15733). If they disagree, explain why, for example a missing Sommerfeld effect or non-higgsino couplings.

result.summary:
Relic densities for a higgsino-like dark matter candidate (compute_relic_density with is_higgsino=true; the tool sets the annihilation cross section automatically): Omega h^2 = 0.0731, 0.0898, 0.1083, 0.1285 and 0.1503 at m = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV (tc-...-23/25/27/29/31). The curve reaches the Planck value of 0.120 at about 1158 GeV, +/-6 GeV from the server's +/-0.0012 Planck band (the brief's +/-0.001 gives about +/-5 GeV). A direct call at 1159 GeV returns 0.120 (tc-...-33). This is inside the 1.08-1.2 TeV literature range. It is about 60-80 GeV above the 1.08-1.1 TeV values (2609.02775, 2609.02608) and close to the about 1.2 TeV value (2410.15733), so agreement is only partial.

Physics in the tool: the higgsino setting is a simple scaling of the cross section, sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s x (1100 GeV/m)^2, fed into a Kolb-Turner freeze-out estimate (x_f about 24.5, g* = 86.25). There is no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch; the only inputs are m_chi_GeV, is_higgsino and sigma_v_cm3_s. As a result, the with/without-Sommerfeld comparison (step 3) and the splitting-sensitivity runs (step 4) could not be done with compute_relic_density. Its closeness to the literature reflects how it was calibrated, not a full calculation.

Constraint checks (check_all_constraints): at 1100 GeV with delta = 400, 566 and 1000 keV, and at 1159 GeV with delta = 400 keV, every point is rated VIABLE. In each case Fermi-LAT and Planck CMB show no exclusion, sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2 and N_expected_LZ = 0.00 (tc-...-32/33/34/35). The relic verdict passes at 1100 GeV despite the tool's own 9.8 sigma tension.

Caveats:
- The pass/consistent flags are True even at 7-25 sigma tension, which looks like a bug.
- N_LZ = 0 at delta = 400 keV conflicts with the literature, where splittings of about 340-380 keV give about one event (posted as q-06).
- The indirect-detection treatment assumes p-wave annihilation suppressed by the mass splitting, giving sigma_v of about 1e-41 cm^3/s today. That is inappropriate for an s-wave, Sommerfeld-enhanced higgsino.

Posted as findings f-001 and f-002 and question q-06. No figures or files were produced.

result.summary: The inelastic-DM server models the higgsino with Z exchange (sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2), the LZ 2.84 t-yr extended nuclear-recoil window, and a halo cutoff of v_esc + v_E = 776 km/s (tc-...-20, -21). At m_chi = 1100 GeV, the expected LZ event counts are: 744.6 at delta = 300 keV (grossly excluded against 1 observed event); 1.97 at 350 keV (P(N>=1) = 0.86, peak recoil energy E_R = 315 keV); and 0.00 at 380, 500, 566 and 700 keV, where the spectrum would peak at 342, 450, 510 and 630 keV (finding f-003). At delta = 380 keV the result does not depend much on mass: the minimum speed needed for the 248 keV event is v_min = 802, 799 and 796 km/s at m = 1000, 1100 and 1200 GeV, all above 776 km/s and so out of reach. Xenon's kinematic reach, worked by hand: delta_max = mu v_max^2/2, with mu = 109.8 GeV. That gives about 368 keV for v_max = 776 km/s and about 385 keV for 544+250 km/s, consistent with the tool's cutoff between 350 and 380 keV (f-004). The scan over m = 800-1400 GeV and delta = 0-800 keV (17x17 points) found 144 of 289 points viable and 9 points predicting 0.3-5 LZ events. Its best fit is m = 988 GeV, delta = 350 keV. Files: /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz and constraint_summary.png (f-005, f-006). The recoil spectrum plot for 1100 GeV, 380 keV is at /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/recoil_spectrum.png. Annual modulation at 1100 GeV, 350 keV and E_R = 248 keV: 98.5% amplitude, peaking on June 2; the event date of September 1 sees 22.5% of the peak rate. Regions at 1.1 TeV: delta below about 340 keV is excluded by xenon (hundreds of events predicted); delta of about 345-368 keV is allowed and can explain the 248 keV event (tool value); delta above about 370 keV is out of xenon's reach. The literature solar-capture bound (delta > 566 keV, 2609.02775) therefore puts every solar-capture-allowed thermal higgsino out of LZ inelastic reach under the Standard Halo Model.
result.block_reason: Open items: (1) The tool gives only total counts, with no breakdown into the [14,225), [225,271] and (271,800] keV bins. (2) The scan and plot files went to the server's default directory, not the run directory, because the tools have no output_dir parameter. (3) The 566 keV and literature 340-380 keV bands were not drawn on the plot; the plotting tool has no overlay option. (4) Halo-parameter sensitivity (q-04) was not tested, because the tool exposes no v0 or v_esc parameters.

issues.text: Over budget. As written it needs about 15 calls: 1 describe + 5 relic + 3 Sommerfeld toggles + 3 delta checks + 2 check_all. Drop the delta-sensitivity step. Keep the Sommerfeld toggle only if describe_tools shows a switch exists. This brings it to about 9-11 calls.

The serve-idm server is probably a generic inelastic-DM model, not a pure higgsino with SU(2) couplings, Sommerfeld enhancement and full coannihilation. If describe_tools does not state higgsino electroweak couplings and Sommerfeld enhancement, label the results as a toy model. In that case, do not report a 'higgsino Planck-crossing mass'. Report only the tool's crossing mass and how far it sits from the 1.0-1.2 TeV literature target. Quote the tool's model description verbatim.

The delta-sensitivity step (0.3, 0.566, 1.0 MeV) is physically uninformative. A sub-MeV splitting is far below T_f of about m/20, which is about 50 GeV, so the relic density should not depend on delta. If the tool does show delta dependence, that indicates a modelling artifact and should be reported as one. Check whether delta is entered in keV or MeV before calling.

The hand calculation of delta_max must use the xenon reduced mass, about 110 GeV at m = 1.1 TeV (m_N about 122 GeV), not the DM mass. This gives delta_max of about 0.5 * 110 GeV * (794/3e5)^2, which is about 385 keV. That is already below the LMC-preferred 480-520 keV and below the 566 keV solar bound. This is an important consistency check on the literature claims. Show the arithmetic explicitly and use the tool's own v0 and v_esc. Do not report an unshown number.

The LZ limit built into the tool is probably the earlier WS2022/2024 result, not the 2026 2.84 t-yr extended window. The tool also has no XENONnT limit. State which exposure and energy window the tool uses. Do not attribute tool exclusions to 2609.02823. Binned counts in [14,225), [225,271] and (271,800] keV are feasible only if predict_recoil returns a spectrum file that can be loaded with load_table_data. Otherwise report the integrated rate only.

Budget is tight, at about 12-13 calls. Drop predict_annual_modulation and the redundant check_all_constraints unless calls remain. Overlay the 566 keV and 340-380 keV literature values only after d-03 confirms that those IDs exist on arXiv.

issues.text: The arithmetic checks out: sigma_v = 2.5e-26 x (1100/m)^2 reproduces 3.73e-26 at 900 GeV, and interpolating between 1100 and 1200 GeV gives about 1158 GeV. However, the tool is a single-channel Kolb-Turner scaling calibrated to 1.1 TeV. The 1158 GeV crossing is a calibration artefact, not a higgsino prediction. The final report must label it as a toy-model crossing, as critique c-01 required.

The scan counts 144 of 289 points as viable. That count uses the same relic 'passes' flag that returns True at 7-25 sigma tension, so it probably includes points that are far from the Planck abundance. It also relies on the p-wave-suppressed indirect-detection model, which is wrong for a higgsino. The viable fraction should not be quoted as physics until it is recomputed with a correct relic criterion.

The best fit at m = 988 GeV, delta = 350 keV fits the LZ event, not the thermal relic. With the tool's own relic curve, 988 GeV gives Omega h^2 of about 0.087, which is under-abundant. The best fit is therefore not a full-abundance thermal higgsino, and this should be stated.

The count falls from 744.6 at 300 keV to 1.97 at 350 keV to 0 at 380 keV. That steep drop comes from the hard cutoff v_esc + v_E = 776 km/s. The literature uses about 544 + 250 km/s, roughly 794 km/s (giving delta_max of about 385 keV), and fits delta of about 377 keV (2609.02608) or 339 keV (2609.26698). The tool's lower velocity cutoff probably explains q-06. The splitting that gives one event depends strongly on halo assumptions, and this has not been tested.
